subtopics.title: DataWeave Array Functions Reference
subtopics.meta_description: A DataWeave 2.0 array function reference covering map, filter, reduce, flatMap, pluck, orderBy, groupBy, distinctBy and more, with fully worked examples.
subtopics.summary: A reference of the most commonly used DataWeave 2.0 array functions, each explained with a worked input-to-output example.
subtopics.content_html:
Arrays are the data shape you touch most often in integration work — lists of orders, records from a database query, rows from a CSV. DataWeave's core module ships a rich set of array functions that cover mapping, filtering, aggregating and reshaping without ever needing a manual loop. This page collects the ones you will reach for constantly, each with a short description and a working example.

FunctionDescriptionExample
mapTransforms each element, producing a new array of the same length[1,2,3] map ($ * 2) → [2,4,6]
filterKeeps only elements matching a condition[1,2,3,4] filter ($ mod 2 == 0) → [2,4]
reduceFolds an array down to a single accumulated value[1,2,3] reduce ((item, acc=0) -> acc + item) → 6
flatMapMaps then flattens one level of nested arrays[[1,2],[3]] flatMap ($ map $ * 10) → [10,20,30]
pluckExtracts key, value or index triples (also works on arrays of objects)payload pluck .price
orderBySorts elements by a derived key, ascending by defaultpayload orderBy $.age
groupByBuckets elements into an object keyed by a derived valuepayload groupBy $.status
distinctByRemoves duplicate elements based on a derived keypayload distinctBy $.email
joinByJoins array elements into a single string with a separator["a","b","c"] joinBy "-" → "a-b-c"
sizeOfReturns the number of elements in an arraysizeOf [1,2,3] → 3
flattenCollapses nested arrays into a single flat arrayflatten [[1,2],[3,[4]]] → [1,2,3,[4]]
zip / unzipPairs up elements from parallel arrays, or reverses that pairing[1,2] zip ["a","b"] → [[1,"a"],[2,"b"]]
some / everyTests whether any or all elements satisfy a condition[1,2,3] every ($ > 0) → true
splitBySplits an array (or string) into chunks around a matcher[1,2,0,3] splitBy ($ == 0)

Example 1: Shaping an Order List

A typical integration step takes a raw array of order records, filters out cancelled ones, and reshapes each surviving record.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var orders = [
  { id: 1, status: "COMPLETE", total: 42.50 },
  { id: 2, status: "CANCELLED", total: 10.00 },
  { id: 3, status: "COMPLETE", total: 99.90 }
]
---
orders
  filter ($.status == "COMPLETE")
  map (o) -> { orderId: o.id, amountDue: o.total }

/* Output:
[
  { "orderId": 1, "amountDue": 42.5 },
  { "orderId": 3, "amountDue": 99.9 }
]
*/

Example 2: Aggregating Totals with reduce

reduce is the general-purpose tool for turning an array into a single value, such as a running total or a concatenated string.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var totals = [42.50, 10.00, 99.90]
---
{
  grandTotal: totals reduce ((amount, acc=0) -> acc + amount)
}

/* Output:
{ "grandTotal": 152.4 }
*/

Example 3: Grouping and Deduplicating

groupBy and distinctBy both take a key-selector lambda and are frequently combined with pluck or map immediately afterward to reshape the resulting buckets.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var customers = [
  { id: 1, region: "EMEA" },
  { id: 2, region: "APAC" },
  { id: 3, region: "EMEA" }
]
---
customers groupBy $.region

/* Output:
{
  "EMEA": [ { "id": 1, "region": "EMEA" }, { "id": 3, "region": "EMEA" } ],
  "APAC": [ { "id": 2, "region": "APAC" } ]
}
*/

Key Points

  • map and filter are the two functions you will reach for the most; both preserve or shrink the array without changing its overall shape.
  • reduce is the escape hatch for any aggregation that isn't already a built-in function — sums, string joins, custom accumulators.
  • groupBy and orderBy both take a key-selector, not a full comparator, which keeps common cases concise.
  • flatten only removes one level of nesting per call; nest calls or use flatMap for deeper structures.
  • Most array functions are non-mutating — they always return a new array, leaving the original untouched.

Chaining Array Functions

DataWeave's pipeline-friendly syntax makes it natural to chain several array functions in sequence, reading top to bottom as a series of steps rather than nested calls. A common pattern is filter, then map, then orderBy, which mirrors how you would describe the transformation in plain English: take the completed orders, extract just the fields needed, and sort them by date. Because each function returns a new array, chaining does not require intermediate variables, though naming an intermediate step with a var can still help readability in longer pipelines.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var orders = [
  { id: 1, status: "COMPLETE", placedOn: |2026-08-01|, total: 42.50 },
  { id: 2, status: "CANCELLED", placedOn: |2026-08-05|, total: 10.00 },
  { id: 3, status: "COMPLETE", placedOn: |2026-07-15|, total: 99.90 }
]
---
orders
  filter ($.status == "COMPLETE")
  map (o) -> { orderId: o.id, placedOn: o.placedOn, total: o.total }
  orderBy $.placedOn

/* Output:
[
  { "orderId": 3, "placedOn": "2026-07-15", "total": 99.9 },
  { "orderId": 1, "placedOn": "2026-08-01", "total": 42.5 }
]
*/

subtopics.title: DataWeave Object Functions Reference
subtopics.meta_description: A DataWeave 2.0 object function reference covering mapObject, pluck, entrySet, valuesOf, namesOf, mergeWith and filterObject, with fully worked examples.
subtopics.summary: A reference of the DataWeave 2.0 functions used to transform, inspect and merge object structures, illustrated with worked examples.
subtopics.content_html:
Objects in DataWeave are ordered collections of key-value pairs, and unlike many languages, keys are not required to be unique — a fact that shapes how several of these functions behave. This reference covers the functions you need to reshape objects, inspect their keys and values, and merge two objects together.

FunctionDescriptionExample
mapObjectTransforms each key-value pair, returning a new object{a:1,b:2} mapObject (v,k) -> { (k): v * 10 }
pluckExtracts keys, values, or indices from an object into arrays{a:1,b:2} pluck $ → [1,2]
entrySet / entriesOfReturns an array of {key, value} entry objectsentriesOf({a:1}) → [{key:"a",value:1}]
valuesOfReturns just the values of an object as an arrayvaluesOf({a:1,b:2}) → [1,2]
namesOf / keysOfReturns just the key names of an object as an arraynamesOf({a:1,b:2}) → ["a","b"]
mergeWithMerges two objects, with the right-hand object's keys winning on conflicts{a:1,b:2} mergeWith {b:99} → {a:1,b:99}
filterObjectKeeps only key-value pairs matching a condition{a:1,b:2} filterObject (v,k) -> v > 1

Example 1: Renaming and Recomputing Values with mapObject

mapObject is the object counterpart to map: the lambda receives value, key (and optionally index), and returns a single-entry object that gets merged into the result — which is also how you rename keys on the fly.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var prices = { widgetPrice: 10, gadgetPrice: 25 }
---
prices mapObject (value, key) -> {
  (key replace "Price" with "PriceWithTax"): value * 1.2
}

/* Output:
{ "widgetPriceWithTax": 12, "gadgetPriceWithTax": 30 }
*/

Example 2: Inspecting an Object's Shape

namesOf, valuesOf and entriesOf are handy whenever you need to treat an object generically — for example, building a summary of an unknown payload's fields.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var record = { id: 7, name: "Ada", active: true }
---
{
  fieldNames: namesOf(record),
  fieldCount: sizeOf(namesOf(record)),
  entries: entriesOf(record)
}

/* Output:
{
  "fieldNames": ["id", "name", "active"],
  "fieldCount": 3,
  "entries": [
    { "key": "id", "value": 7 },
    { "key": "name", "value": "Ada" },
    { "key": "active", "value": true }
  ]
}
*/

Example 3: Merging Defaults with Overrides

mergeWith is a clean way to layer a set of overrides on top of a defaults object without writing manual conditional logic, and filterObject can trim the result afterward.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var defaults = { retries: 3, timeoutMs: 5000, debug: false }
var overrides = { timeoutMs: 8000, debug: true }
---
(defaults mergeWith overrides) filterObject (value, key) -> value != false

/* Output:
{ "retries": 3, "timeoutMs": 8000, "debug": true }
*/

Key Points

  • mapObject lets you change keys, values, or both in a single pass, since the lambda returns a whole key-value pair.
  • pluck and valuesOf/namesOf both extract data from objects but pluck can target keys, values or indices depending on the selector used.
  • mergeWith is right-biased: the argument object's keys overwrite the caller's on conflicts.
  • Because DataWeave objects can hold duplicate keys, functions like entriesOf preserve every entry rather than collapsing to a map.
  • filterObject mirrors filter for arrays, but its lambda receives both the value and the key.

A Note on Duplicate Keys

DataWeave objects are ordered sequences of key-value pairs rather than strict maps, so two entries can legally share the same key. This matters for functions like valuesOf and entriesOf, which will faithfully return every entry, duplicates included, whereas a naive property lookup such as obj.key only ever returns the first matching value. When a source system emits repeated keys (a common quirk of XML converted to DataWeave objects, where repeated child elements become repeated keys) use obj.*key to select every value for that key as an array, rather than relying on the single-value selector.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var xmlLike = { item: "Widget", item: "Gadget", item: "Gizmo" }
---
{
  firstOnly: xmlLike.item,
  allValues: xmlLike.*item,
  count: sizeOf(xmlLike.*item)
}

/* Output:
{
  "firstOnly": "Widget",
  "allValues": ["Widget", "Gadget", "Gizmo"],
  "count": 3
}
*/

subtopics.title: DataWeave String Functions Reference
subtopics.meta_description: A DataWeave 2.0 string function reference covering upper, lower, trim, splitBy, contains, camelize, replace, matches, leftPad and more, with examples.
subtopics.summary: A reference of frequently used DataWeave 2.0 string functions for casing, trimming, splitting, matching and padding text values.
subtopics.content_html:
String manipulation shows up constantly in integration flows: normalizing case before a comparison, cleaning up whitespace from a legacy system, validating a format with a regular expression, or padding an identifier to a fixed width for a fixed-length flat file. DataWeave's string functions cover all of these without reaching for a scripting language.

FunctionDescriptionExample
upper / lowerConverts a string to upper or lower caseupper("abc") → "ABC"
trimRemoves leading and trailing whitespacetrim(" hi ") → "hi"
splitBySplits a string into an array around a matcher"a,b,c" splitBy "," → ["a","b","c"]
joinByJoins an array of strings back into one string["a","b"] joinBy "-" → "a-b"
containsTests whether a string contains a substring"hello" contains "ell" → true
startsWith / endsWithTests the beginning or end of a string"invoice.pdf" endsWith ".pdf" → true
camelizeConverts snake_case or kebab-case to camelCasecamelize("order_id") → "orderId"
replaceReplaces matched text with a replacement"2026-08-20" replace "-" with "/"
matchesTests a string against a regular expression"abc123" matches /^[a-z]+[0-9]+$/ → true
leftPad / rightPadPads a string to a fixed length"7" leftPad 4 with "0" → "0007"
substringExtracts a portion of a string by index"hello world" [0 to 4] → "hello"

Example 1: Normalizing Incoming Field Names

Legacy systems frequently emit snake_case or ALL CAPS field names. Combining lower, camelize and trim is a common first step before mapping fields into a clean canonical model.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var raw = { "CUSTOMER_ID ": 501, " first_name": "Ada " }
---
raw mapObject (value, key) -> {
  (camelize(trim(lower(key)))): if (value is String) trim(value) else value
}

/* Output:
{ "customerId": 501, "firstName": "Ada" }
*/

Example 2: Validating and Reformatting an Identifier

matches is useful for guarding a transformation with a validation check, while leftPad normalizes width for downstream systems that expect fixed-length codes.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var skus = ["7", "842", "15"]
---
skus map (sku) -> {
  original: sku,
  isNumeric: sku matches /^[0-9]+$/,
  padded: sku leftPad 5 with "0"
}

/* Output:
[
  { "original": "7", "isNumeric": true, "padded": "00007" },
  { "original": "842", "isNumeric": true, "padded": "00842" },
  { "original": "15", "isNumeric": true, "padded": "00015" }
]
*/

Example 3: Splitting and Rejoining a Delimited Value

splitBy and joinBy are frequently paired when reformatting a delimited value, such as converting a comma-separated tag list into a pipe-separated one after trimming each entry.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var tagString = "urgent, billing , escalated"
---
(tagString splitBy ",") map (t) -> trim(t) joinBy " | "

/* Output:
"urgent | billing | escalated"
*/

Key Points

  • upper, lower, trim and camelize are commonly chained together when normalizing field names or values from legacy sources.
  • splitBy and joinBy work as an inverse pair for delimited strings, similar to their array counterparts.
  • matches takes a regular expression literal (/pattern/), not a string, and returns a boolean.
  • leftPad/rightPad are essential when producing fixed-width output for flat files or legacy record formats.
  • Most string functions are case- and locale-sensitive; use upper/lower explicitly before comparisons when case should not matter.

Chaining String Transformations Safely

String functions compose cleanly, but real payloads are rarely as clean as the examples above — a field might be null, or a number might arrive typed as a String. Wrapping a chain of string functions with a null check (or a default fallback) avoids runtime errors when a field is missing entirely, and casting explicitly with as String avoids type-mismatch errors when the underlying value is not already text.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var records = [
  { code: "  ab-12 " },
  { code: null },
  { code: 4500 }
]
---
records map (r) -> {
  cleaned: upper(trim(r.code default "" as String))
}

/* Output:
[
  { "cleaned": "AB-12" },
  { "cleaned": "" },
  { "cleaned": "4500" }
]
*/

subtopics.title: DataWeave Date, Time and Number Functions Reference
subtopics.meta_description: A DataWeave 2.0 reference for date and time handling with now, the | operator, daysBetween, date arithmetic and number functions like round and random.
subtopics.summary: A reference of DataWeave 2.0 functions and operators for working with dates, times and numbers, shown with worked examples.
subtopics.content_html:
Dates and numbers each have their own quirks in any transformation language, and DataWeave provides a focused set of functions and operators to handle both: converting between string formats, measuring elapsed time, and rounding or randomizing numeric values. This page covers the ones you will use most in day-to-day integration work.

Function / OperatorDescriptionExample
now()Returns the current DateTime including timezonenow() → 2026-08-20T14:03:00Z
asCasts/parses or formats a value using a target type and format"2026-08-20" as Date {format: "yyyy-MM-dd"}
| (format operator)Formats a Date/DateTime/Time value using a pattern stringnow() as String {format: "dd/MM/yyyy"}
daysBetweenReturns whole days between two datesdaysBetween(\|2026-01-01\|, \|2026-01-11\|) → 10
+ / - on PeriodAdds or subtracts a Period from a date/time value\|2026-01-01\| + \|P7D\|
roundRounds a number to the nearest integerround(4.6) → 5
ceil / floorRounds up or down to the nearest integerceil(4.1) → 5, floor(4.9) → 4
random()Returns a pseudo-random Number between 0 and 1random()
isDecimalTests whether a Number has a non-zero decimal partisDecimal(4.5) → true

Example 1: Formatting a Timestamp for an Outbound API

Incoming and outgoing systems rarely agree on date format. DataWeave's date literals (\|value\|) combined with the as operator handle both parsing and formatting.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var orderPlaced = |2026-08-20T09:15:00Z|
---
{
  isoTimestamp: orderPlaced as String,
  displayDate: orderPlaced as String {format: "MMM d, yyyy"},
  compactDate: orderPlaced as String {format: "yyyyMMdd"}
}

/* Output:
{
  "isoTimestamp": "2026-08-20T09:15:00Z",
  "displayDate": "Aug 20, 2026",
  "compactDate": "20260820"
}
*/

Example 2: Calculating SLA Age with daysBetween

Comparing two dates to compute an elapsed duration is a common requirement for SLA and aging reports.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var ticket = { opened: |2026-08-01|, dueInDays: 14 }
var today = |2026-08-20|
---
{
  ageInDays: daysBetween(ticket.opened, today),
  dueDate: ticket.opened + |P14D|,
  isOverdue: daysBetween(ticket.opened, today) > ticket.dueInDays
}

/* Output:
{
  "ageInDays": 19,
  "dueDate": "2026-08-15",
  "isOverdue": true
}
*/

Example 3: Rounding Prices and Flagging Fractional Quantities

Number functions like round, ceil, floor and isDecimal are common in pricing and inventory calculations where fractional units need special handling.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var lines = [
  { sku: "A1", qty: 3.5, unitPrice: 9.995 },
  { sku: "B2", qty: 2, unitPrice: 14.499 }
]
---
lines map (line) -> {
  sku: line.sku,
  roundedPrice: round(line.unitPrice * 100) / 100,
  wholeUnitsNeeded: ceil(line.qty),
  hasPartialQuantity: isDecimal(line.qty)
}

/* Output:
[
  { "sku": "A1", "roundedPrice": 10.0, "wholeUnitsNeeded": 4, "hasPartialQuantity": true },
  { "sku": "B2", "roundedPrice": 14.5, "wholeUnitsNeeded": 2, "hasPartialQuantity": false }
]
*/

Key Points

  • Date, Time and DateTime literals are written between pipes, like \|2026-08-20\|, and are distinct types from strings.
  • The as operator handles both parsing a string into a date type and formatting a date type back into a string, driven by the format option.
  • daysBetween and Period arithmetic (+/- with \|P...\| literals) cover the majority of duration calculations without manual math.
  • round, ceil and floor all return integers but differ in rounding direction, which matters for billing and inventory logic.
  • isDecimal is a quick guard for distinguishing whole quantities from fractional ones before applying business rules.

Working Across Time Zones

DateTime literals carry a timezone offset, and DataWeave preserves it through arithmetic rather than silently normalizing to UTC. When comparing or displaying timestamps from systems in different zones, convert explicitly rather than assuming two DateTime values are already aligned. The as operator combined with a {format: ...} option and a timezone-aware pattern lets you render the same instant in a specific zone for display, while comparisons and duration math continue to operate on the underlying instant correctly regardless of the zone each value was written in.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var meetingUtc = |2026-08-20T18:00:00Z|
var submittedLocal = |2026-08-20T14:00:00-04:00|
---
{
  sameInstant: meetingUtc == submittedLocal,
  utcDisplay: meetingUtc as String {format: "HH:mm 'UTC'"},
  localZoneDisplay: submittedLocal as String {format: "HH:mm xxx"}
}

/* Output:
{
  "sameInstant": true,
  "utcDisplay": "18:00 UTC",
  "localZoneDisplay": "14:00 -04:00"
}
*/

subtopics.title: DataWeave Core Module Functions (read, write, flatten and more)
subtopics.meta_description: A DataWeave 2.0 reference for core module functions including read, write, flatten, mapObject vs map, typeOf, isEmpty, sizeOf and the default operator.
subtopics.summary: A reference of foundational DataWeave 2.0 core module functions used for dynamic parsing, serialization, type inspection and null-safe defaults.
subtopics.content_html:
Beyond the array, object and string helpers, DataWeave's core module includes a handful of foundational functions that show up in almost every non-trivial transform: dynamically parsing and serializing data, inspecting a value's runtime type, checking for emptiness, and safely falling back to a default when a value is missing.

Function / OperatorDescriptionExample
read()Parses a string (or binary) into structured data using a given MIME typeread(payload, "application/json")
write()Serializes structured data into a string using a given MIME typewrite(payload, "application/xml")
flattenCollapses one level of nested arrays into a single arrayflatten [[1,2],[3]] → [1,2,3]
mapObject vs mapmap iterates arrays; mapObject iterates key-value pairs of objectssee comparison below
typeOfReturns the runtime type of a valuetypeOf(1) → Number
isEmptyTests whether a string, array or object has no contentisEmpty([]) → true
sizeOfReturns length/count for strings, arrays and objectssizeOf("abc") → 3
defaultSubstitutes a fallback value when the left side is nullpayload.discount default 0

Example 1: Parsing an Embedded JSON String with read()

APIs sometimes embed a JSON or XML document as a plain string field. read() parses that string on demand so you can navigate it just like any other structured value.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var event = {
  eventId: "evt-1",
  payloadJson: "{\"orderId\": 88, \"total\": 120.5}"
}
---
{
  eventId: event.eventId,
  orderId: read(event.payloadJson, "application/json").orderId,
  total: read(event.payloadJson, "application/json").total
}

/* Output:
{ "eventId": "evt-1", "orderId": 88, "total": 120.5 }
*/

Example 2: Serializing to XML with write()

write() is the inverse of read(): it takes structured data and produces a string in the target format, which is useful when you need a formatted string mid-flow rather than relying on the transform's output directive alone.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var order = { id: 1, item: "Widget", qty: 3 }
---
{
  orderId: order.id,
  xmlSnippet: write(order, "application/xml", { writeDeclaration: false })
}

/* Output (xmlSnippet is a string containing):
{
  "orderId": 1,
  "xmlSnippet": "<order><id>1</id><item>Widget</item><qty>3</qty></order>"
}
*/

Example 3: Defensive Defaults, Emptiness and Type Checks

The default operator, isEmpty and typeOf are commonly combined to write transforms that tolerate missing or oddly-shaped upstream data without throwing errors.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var customer = { name: "Ada", tags: [], discountCode: null }
---
{
  name: customer.name default "Unknown",
  hasTags: !isEmpty(customer.tags),
  discountCode: customer.discountCode default "NONE",
  nameType: typeOf(customer.name)
}

/* Output:
{
  "name": "Ada",
  "hasTags": false,
  "discountCode": "NONE",
  "nameType": "String"
}
*/

mapObject vs. map: Choosing the Right Iterator

map iterates an array, calling the lambda with each element (and optional index), and always returns an array. mapObject iterates an object's key-value pairs, calling the lambda with value, key (and optional index), and always returns an object, since the lambda must return a single-entry object for each pair. Reaching for the wrong one is a common source of type errors for developers new to DataWeave — if you are iterating payload.items (an array of orders) you want map; if you are iterating the fields of one order object itself, you want mapObject.

Key Points

  • read() and write() let you parse or serialize data dynamically mid-transform, independent of the script's top-level output directive.
  • flatten only removes one level of array nesting per call; deeply nested arrays need repeated or recursive flattening.
  • map operates on arrays and returns arrays; mapObject operates on objects and returns objects — they are not interchangeable.
  • default only kicks in for null, not for empty strings or empty arrays, so pair it with isEmpty checks when those also need a fallback.
  • typeOf and sizeOf are useful defensive tools when a transform must handle payloads whose shape is not fully guaranteed.

sizeOf Across Different Types

sizeOf is polymorphic: on a String it returns character count, on an Array it returns element count, and on an Object it returns the number of key-value pairs (counting duplicate keys separately). This single function replaces the need for type-specific length checks in most validation logic, though it is worth remembering that it throws an error if called on a type that has no defined notion of size, such as a Number or Boolean, so guard with typeOf first when the input's shape is not already known.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var samples = ["hello", [1,2,3,4], { a: 1, b: 2 }]
---
samples map (s) -> {
  type: typeOf(s),
  size: sizeOf(s)
}

/* Output:
[
  { "type": "String", "size": 5 },
  { "type": "Array", "size": 4 },
  { "type": "Object", "size": 2 }
]
*/
